about: Hand-authored classic spots. Every number shown to the user is recomputed by the engine from these inputs; 'claims' store the engine's values and tests/library.test.ts fails if they drift. Text placeholders: {equity} {required} {outs} {clean} {next} {byRiver} {combos} {ev} {spr} {alpha:NN} {mdf}. Range strings starting with @ reference a chart in src/data/charts.ts (optionally :action).

spots.title: C-bet on a dry king-high board
spots.history: You open 2.5bb on the BTN, BB calls. BB checks.

villain.label: BB's full defending range vs a BTN open

why: K-7-2 rainbow favours the preflop raiser: you hold more strong kings, while the BB's calling range is full of weak, unconnected hands.
With a range advantage on a static board, bet small and often. A 33% bet only has to work {alpha:33} of the time as a pure bluff.
Your A-high has {equity} equity vs BB's whole range: it can win at showdown, but a small bet folds out better hands like small pairs.
assumptions: 6-max, 100bb. BB defends the Poker Skill BB-vs-BTN range (no 3-bets modelled).
spots.exploit: Against players who call c-bets with any pair, give up more often with pure air and bet your value hands bigger.

spots.title: Wet, connected board that hits the caller
spots.history: You open 2.5bb on the BTN, BB calls. BB checks.

villain.label: BB's full defending range vs a BTN open

why: 9-8-6 two-tone connects with the BB's suited connectors, gappers and small pairs: the range advantage shifts toward the caller.
AK has no pair and no draw here ({equity} vs BB's range). Betting big folds the hands you beat and gets called or raised by the hands that beat you.
Checking keeps the pot small and realizes your overcard equity for free.
assumptions: 6-max, 100bb. BB defends the Poker Skill BB-vs-BTN range.
spots.exploit: Loose home-game callers rarely fold on boards like this — c-bet bluffs here are especially poor.

spots.title: Set on a draw-heavy board
spots.history: You open 2.5bb on the BTN, BB calls. BB checks.

villain.label: BB's continuing range: top pair or better plus flush/straight draws

why: You have the second-best possible hand and many worse hands continue: 9x, flush draws, straight draws, pair + draw.
Against that continuing range you have {equity} equity. Draws have real equity against you, so charge them now (protection) and build the pot (value).
Slow-playing on a wet board gives free cards to exactly the hands that can outdraw you.
assumptions: 6-max, 100bb. Equity measured vs BB hands that would call a bet: top pair or better, flush draws and open-enders.
spots.exploit: Home-game players love to call with draws and any pair — size up rather than down.

spots.title: Overpair on a low, dry board
spots.history: You open 2.5bb in the CO, BTN calls, blinds fold. You act first.

villain.label: BTN's flat-calling range vs a CO open

why: QQ is way ahead of the button's calling range ({equity}): mostly overcards, smaller pairs and suited connectors.
Bet for value: many pairs (22–TT, 8x, 5x) and overcards with backdoors will call a medium bet.
Checking out of position invites a free card for two overcards that have about six outs against you.
assumptions: 6-max, 100bb. BTN's calling range from Poker Skill's BTN-vs-CO chart (its 3-bet hands removed).

spots.title: Thin value on the river
spots.history: You open 2.5bb on the BTN, BB calls. Flop: BB checks, you bet 1.8, BB calls. Turn: check, check. River: BB checks.

villain.label: BB's check-calling range: any pair using a hole card

why: Top pair, jack kicker is ahead of most of the hands that called the flop and checked twice ({equity} vs that range): K8–K2, 9x, 5x, pocket pairs.
A small bet gets called by many of those worse hands; a big bet only gets called by kings with better kickers and two pairs.
Thin value = betting when you are only modestly ahead of the calling range.
assumptions: Full ring line, 100bb. BB's range: Poker Skill BB defend range filtered to any pair using a hole card (missed draws assumed to have folded or will fold).
The BB defend range comes from a 6-max chart, used as an approximation at a full table.
spots.exploit: Against calling stations, bet bigger for value with top pair — they call with any piece. Against tight players, a check is fine.

spots.title: River nut flush: get paid
spots.history: BTN open, BB call. Flop: BB checks, you bet 1.8, BB calls. Turn: BB checks, you bet 6.8, BB calls. River: BB checks.

villain.label: BB's range after calling two bets: any pair or better

why: You have the nut flush ({equity} vs BB's calling range — only a straight flush beats you).
Bet big: kings, two pairs, sets and smaller flushes can call. Checking wins nothing extra.
When you hold the nuts and the opponent's range is capped, bigger sizes make more money from the hands that do call.
assumptions: 6-max, 100bb, BB's range filtered to pair or better.
spots.exploit: In home games, people rarely fold a flush or two pair on the river. Don't be afraid of a pot-size bet.

spots.title: Ace-high with showdown value
spots.history: BTN open, BB call. Flop: you c-bet 1.8, BB calls. Turn: check, check. River: BB checks.

villain.label: BB's check-call then check-check range: pairs plus missed heart draws

why: Ace-high beats missed draws (Q-J, J-T, 5-x hearts) that would fold to a bet anyway.
Hands that call a bet — any pair — all beat you. Betting turns a hand with showdown value into a bluff.
Checking wins whenever villain has a missed draw: here {equity} of the time vs the stated range.
assumptions: Villain's range: pair or better, plus half of their no-pair hands (missed draws).

spots.title: Top pair, top kicker on a blank turn
spots.history: BTN open, BB call. Flop: BB checks, you bet 1.8, BB calls. Turn: BB checks.

villain.label: BB's flop check-calling range: any pair or a draw

why: AK is ahead of nearly everything that called the flop ({equity}): weaker kings, 7x, pocket pairs.
The 5 changes little. Bet again for value — worse kings and pairs still call; giving a free card helps gutshots and overcards.
Checking is not a disaster (pot control), but it loses value against a range full of worse pairs.
assumptions: BB's range: pairs using a hole card plus open-enders/flush draws from the defend range.

spots.title: Middle pair in position: pot control
spots.history: BTN open, BB call. Flop: BB checks, you bet 1.8, BB calls. Turn: BB checks.

villain.label: BB's flop check-calling range: any pair or a draw

why: Second pair has {equity} vs the hands that called the flop: you beat draws and weaker pairs, lose to every jack.
If you bet big, better hands call and worse hands fold — a classic reason to check.
Checking in position realizes your equity and keeps the pot manageable.
assumptions: BB range as stated; one more street to come.

spots.title: Top pair in the BB: let the raiser bet
spots.history: BTN opens 2.5bb, you call in the BB. You act first on the flop.

villain.label: BTN's opening range

why: On K-7-2 the button has the range advantage and will c-bet very often, including many worse hands.
Your top pair has {equity} vs the button's opening range: you're happy to check and let them bluff, then call or check-raise.
Leading into the preflop raiser on boards that favour them is rarely better than checking.
assumptions: 6-max, 100bb. BTN range = PokerCoaching 6-max BTN RFI chart.

spots.title: C-bet into two opponents
spots.history: You open 2.5bb in the CO, BTN and BB call. BB checks to you; BTN is still to act behind.

villain.label: BTN's calling range (one of the two opponents)

why: A bluff needs every opponent to fold. Even if each folds 60% independently, both fold only 0.6 × 0.6 = 36% of the time.
K-high with no draw has {equity} vs even one caller's range — little equity when called.
Multiway, bet your strong hands and good draws; check most air.
assumptions: Full ring, 100bb. Equity shown vs one opponent's range (BTN flat range) — vs two players it is lower.
The BTN calling range comes from a 6-max chart (no verified free full-ring vs-open chart), used as an approximation.
spots.exploit: Multiway pots in home games are where c-bet bluffs go to die. Bluff even less than theory suggests.

spots.title: Combo draw on the turn: semi-bluff
spots.history: BTN open, BB call. Flop: BB checks, you bet 1.8, BB calls. Turn: BB checks.

villain.label: BB's flop check-calling range: any pair or a draw

why: You have {outs} outs to a straight or flush ({next} to hit on the river) and {equity} equity vs BB's range.
Betting wins immediately when they fold, and you still have a big draw when called: a semi-bluff.
Checking is acceptable (a free look), but it gives up your fold equity.
assumptions: BB's range: any pair or a strong draw after calling the flop.

spots.title: KJo under the gun at a full table
spots.history: You are first to act at a 9-handed table. Blinds 0.5/1.
why: The full-ring UTG chart opens only KQo among offsuit king hands. KJo is a fold.
Eight players act behind you; KJo is often dominated by the AK, AJ and KQ that continue.
Limping is not part of a sound strategy: it invites raises and leaves you out of position in a bloated pot.
assumptions: PokerCoaching full-ring chart (8-handed source; UTG chart used for 9-handed UTG).

spots.title: Small pair under the gun, full ring
spots.history: First to act at a 9-handed table.
why: The source's full-ring UTG range starts at 77+: 66 is a fold there (it opens from LJ onward).
Small pairs mostly win by flopping a set (11.8% of flops) and need deep stacks and few opponents behind.
In 6-max the same seat opens 66+ — table size matters.
assumptions: PokerCoaching full-ring chart (8-handed source).
spots.exploit: If your home game is very passive (few 3-bets, many limpers), opening or limping small pairs early is less costly — but it is not the baseline.

spots.title: Suited connector on the button
spots.history: Folded to you on the button.
why: 76s is inside the 6-max button range (75s+). Raise.
Only the blinds are left and you'll have position: suited connectors play well and steal the blinds often.
assumptions: PokerCoaching 6-max chart, 2.5bb opens.

spots.title: K4o first in from the small blind
spots.history: Folded to you in the small blind.
why: K4o is at the bottom of the source's SB range (K4o+), which says 'raise or call'.
Only the big blind remains; a king-high hand has enough equity to attack one random hand.
Folding gives up a spot the chart plays.
assumptions: PokerCoaching 6-max SB chart ('Raise or Call'); which hands raise vs complete is not given in the free text.

spots.title: Q8o on the button
spots.history: Folded to you on the button.
why: The button range includes Q9o+ but not Q8o: a fold, even on the button.
Weak offsuit queens make second-best pairs and dominated hands far too often.
assumptions: PokerCoaching 6-max chart.

spots.title: A5s under the gun, 6-max
spots.history: First to act at a 6-handed table.
why: The 6-max UTG range includes A3s+, so A5s is an open.
Suited wheel aces make nut flushes and straights and block AA/AK in the hands that play back.
assumptions: PokerCoaching 6-max chart (its first seat is labelled LJ; used as UTG at 6-handed).

spots.title: Top pair, weak kicker vs a check-raise (good price)
spots.history: You open the BTN, BB calls. Flop: BB checks, you bet 1.8, BB check-raises to 6.

villain.label: Value-heavy low-stakes check-raise range: two pair or better, strong kings at half frequency, gutshot bluffs

why: You call 4.2 to win 13.3: you need only {required} equity.
Against this value-heavy range you have {equity}: you're crushed by two pairs and sets, behind KQ/KJ, but well ahead of the gutshot bluffs.
The small raise gives a great price, so even a weak top pair continues once. Re-evaluate on the turn: further big bets from this range mean value.
assumptions: Villain range as stated (an assumption about a typical low-stakes player). No further betting assumed.
spots.exploit: If this player never check-raises as a bluff (only two pair or better), your equity collapses and folding becomes right — that is the read that changes the decision.

spots.title: Set on a flush-draw board vs a shove
spots.history: You open the BTN, BB calls. Flop: BB checks, you bet 1.8, BB shoves all-in for 97.5.

villain.label: BB shoving top pair or better and all flush/straight draws

why: You need {required} to call; you have {equity} against everything they would shove.
Draws are the hands that can beat you, and even a flush draw is a big underdog to top set with two cards to come.
Folding top set here is a large mistake regardless of the exact range.
assumptions: Villain shoves value and draws (stated range). All-in: both remaining cards will be dealt.

spots.title: Overpair vs a check-raise on a wet board
spots.history: You open the CO, BB calls. Flop: BB checks, you bet 1.8, BB check-raises to 6.

villain.label: Two pair or better, plus flush and straight draws at half frequency

why: Price: {required}. Your equity vs the stated range: {equity}.
Sets and two pairs crush you, but draws make up a big part of a check-raising range on 9-8-5 two-tone, and you're ahead of all of them.
With a strong overpair on a wet board, folding to one raise is usually too tight.
assumptions: BB's defend range used as an approximation of a CO-vs-BB defend range. Stated check-raise range.

spots.title: River bluff-catch vs a polar pot bet
spots.history: BTN opens, you call. Flop: you check-call 1.8. Turn: you check-call 6.8. River: you check, BTN bets pot (22.7).

villain.label: Polar: top pair or better for value plus 30% of no-pair hands (missed hearts) as bluffs

why: Facing a pot-size bet you need {required} — exactly one third.
Your top pair, jack kicker wins against bluffs and worse queens: {equity} vs the stated range.
Bluff-catching is a counting exercise: compare how often villain is bluffing (or betting worse) with the price.
assumptions: Villain's river range is an assumption; shown in the Assumptions box. No raise considered profitable here.
spots.exploit: If this player never bluffs rivers (common in home games), this becomes a fold — see the next spot.

spots.title: Same spot vs a player who never bluffs
spots.history: Same line as before: BTN bets pot on the river. This time you know the player only bets the river with strong hands.

villain.label: Value only: two pair or better, plus AQ/KQ

why: Same price ({required}), but against a value-only range your equity drops to {equity}.
Bluff-catchers only make money when bluffs exist. Against players who don't bluff, fold.
This is an exploitative adjustment: the math is identical, the assumed range changed.
assumptions: Villain range: value only (stated read).

spots.title: Nut flush draw vs a half-pot c-bet
spots.history: BTN opens, you call in the BB. Flop: you check, BTN bets 2.8 (half pot).

villain.label: BTN betting top pair or better plus draws

why: Half pot: you need {required}.
Nut flush draw: {outs} outs ({clean} clean), {next} on the turn and {byRiver} by the river if you see both cards. Equity vs the betting range: {equity}.
Easy continue. Raising as a semi-bluff is also reasonable: you have the nut draw and an overcard.
assumptions: Villain bets value and draws (stated). Equity assumes both cards are seen.

spots.title: Gutshot vs a pot-size bet
spots.history: BTN opens, you call. Flop: you check, BTN bets pot (5.5).

villain.label: BTN betting top pair or better plus draws

why: A pot bet asks for {required} equity.
A gutshot has {outs} outs: {next} on the next card. Equity vs the betting range: {equity}.
Not enough — and if the turn misses you face another bet. Fold.
assumptions: Villain range as stated.

spots.title: Open-ender vs a small turn bet
spots.history: CO opens, you call on the BTN. Flop: CO bets 1.8, you call. Turn: CO bets 3 (⅓ pot).

villain.label: CO betting top pair or better plus draws

why: A third-pot bet needs {required}.
{outs} straight outs: {next} on the river. Equity vs the betting range: {equity} — within a point of the price.
On pot odds alone this is break-even, so calling and folding are both fine. Implied odds (getting paid when the straight comes) and position tip it toward calling.
assumptions: Villain range as stated. One card to come.

spots.title: Two overcards vs a ¾-pot c-bet
spots.history: BTN opens, you call. Flop: you check, BTN bets 4.1 (¾ pot).

villain.label: BTN betting top pair or better plus draws

why: A ¾-pot bet requires {required}.
Two overcards have about six outs, some of them not clean. Equity vs a value-and-draws betting range: {equity}.
Against a range that only bets real hands, overcards are not enough; against a frequent c-bettor they can continue.
assumptions: Villain bets only value and draws (no pure air): a tight assumption that makes folding correct more often.
spots.exploit: Many home-game players c-bet every flop. Against them, overcards like AQ can float — the stated range here is a tight bettor.

spots.title: Set mining with 55
spots.history: UTG opens to 2.5bb at a full table, folded to you on the button.

villain.label: Full-ring UTG opening range

why: Raw all-in equity vs UTG's range is {equity} against a price of {required} — slightly above, but preflop raw equity overstates what a small pair realizes after the flop.
The real reason to call is implied odds: you flop a set 11.8% of the time (about 7.5 : 1 against), and with 97.5bb behind a set can win a big pot from overpairs.
In position against a strong, narrow range that pays off, calling is standard at 100bb. With short stacks (little to win when you hit) it becomes a fold.
assumptions: 100bb effective. Graded as an implied-odds call: the immediate equity alone does not justify it.

spots.title: Two pair when the flush comes in
spots.history: BTN opens, you call. Flop: you check-call 1.8. Turn K♥ completes the flush: you check, BTN bets pot (9.1).

villain.label: BTN betting top pair or better (incl. flushes and sets) on the turn

why: Pot bet: you need {required}.
You're ahead of kings and overpairs but behind flushes and sets; you have {outs} outs to a full house. Equity vs the stated range: {equity}.
Turn decisions with one card to come are cleaner: the equity is close to the real outcome if no river bet happens.
assumptions: Villain range as stated (no bluffs).

spots.title: River overbet: top pair with the nut-flush blocker
spots.history: BTN opens, you call. Flop: check-call 1.8. Turn: check-call 6.8. River 7♠: you check, BTN bets 13.7 (60% pot).

villain.label: BTN: two pair or better (incl. flushes) for value plus half of no-pair hands as bluffs

why: You need {required}.
Holding the A♥ means villain can never have the nut flush, and you beat every bluff. Equity vs the stated range: {equity}.
Blockers matter most in polarized river spots like this.
assumptions: Stated polar range. Board has three hearts.

spots.title: Weak pair vs a tiny river bet
spots.history: BTN opens, you call. Flop: check-call 1.8. Turn: check, check. River: you check, BTN bets 2.3 (¼ pot).

villain.label: BTN thin-value betting any pair, plus 30% of no-pair hands

why: A quarter-pot bet needs only {required} equity.
Your pair of sevens beats bluffs and some thin value: {equity} vs the stated range.
Small bets demand very wide defence; folding a pair here is far too tight.
assumptions: Villain range as stated.

spots.title: Top pair + flush draw vs a flop shove
spots.history: BTN opens, you call. Flop: you check, BTN shoves all-in for 97.5.

villain.label: BTN shoving top pair or better plus draws

why: An overbet shove means you need {required}.
Top pair plus a flush draw is strong against value and dominates draws: {equity}.
Call — you're rarely in bad shape, and even against sets you have many outs.
assumptions: Villain shove range as stated. All-in: both cards dealt.

spots.title: Underpair facing a turn barrel
spots.history: BTN opens, you call. Flop: check-call 1.8. Turn: you check, BTN bets 6.8 (¾ pot).

villain.label: BTN double-barrelling top pair or better plus draws

why: You need {required}.
Pocket sixes on K-T-3-8 have two outs to a set and beat only some draws: {equity}.
Fold. Calling down with underpairs against double barrels is a classic leak.
assumptions: Villain range as stated.

spots.title: Flush draw on the turn vs a pot-size bet
spots.history: BTN opens, you call. Flop: check-call 1.8. Turn: you check, BTN bets pot (9.1).

villain.label: BTN betting top pair or better plus draws

why: A pot bet requires {required}.
With one card to come, your {outs} outs hit {next} of the time. Equity vs the range: {equity}.
Not enough on pure pot odds. Calling needs strong implied odds (deep stacks and an opponent who pays off when the flush comes).
assumptions: Villain range as stated. No implied odds counted in the grade.

spots.title: Combo draw vs a flop shove
spots.history: CO opens, you call on the BTN. Flop: CO shoves all-in for 97.5.

villain.label: CO shoving top pair or better only

why: You need {required}.
Open-ended straight draw + flush draw: {outs} outs, {byRiver} to hit by the river, plus overcards. Equity vs their value range: {equity}.
Huge draws are often favourites even against made hands. Call.
assumptions: Villain only shoves value (stated).

spots.title: TPTK vs a river check-raise
spots.history: BTN open, BB call. You bet every street; river: BB checks, you bet 13 into 20, BB check-raises to 39.

villain.label: Low-stakes river check-raise: two pair or better only

why: You need {required}.
Against a river check-raise range of two pair or better, top pair top kicker wins {equity}.
River check-raises at low stakes are overwhelmingly value. Fold, painful as it is.
assumptions: Villain range: value only (stated).
spots.exploit: This is one of the most reliable reads in live low-stakes poker.

spots.title: Second pair vs a small c-bet
spots.history: BTN opens, you call. Flop: you check, BTN bets 1.8 (⅓ pot).

villain.label: BTN c-betting small with its whole opening range

why: A third-pot bet needs only {required}.
Against a range that bets almost everything, second pair has {equity}.
Small c-bets are designed to make you fold hands like this — don't.
assumptions: Villain c-bets the full range (stated).

spots.title: Small pair on a high board vs a tight bettor
spots.history: BTN opens, you call. Flop: you check, BTN bets 2.8 (½ pot).

villain.label: A tight BTN that bets only top pair or better plus draws

why: Half pot: {required} needed.
Pocket fours on K-Q-8 have two outs to a set against a range of kings, queens and draws: {equity}.
Fold. Against a player who also bluffs a lot the math changes — but out of position, underpairs realize their equity poorly on later streets.
assumptions: Villain bets only value and draws (stated read of a tight player).

spots.title: River nuts vs a half-pot bet
spots.history: BTN opens, you call. Flop: check-call 1.8. Turn: check, check. River: you check, BTN bets 4.6 (½ pot).

villain.label: BTN betting any pair or better

why: You flopped the nut straight (8-7-6-5-4) and it's still the nuts: {equity} vs their betting range.
Calling is fine; raising wins more from kings and two pairs that can call.
Value-raise the river when you're far ahead of the betting range.
assumptions: Villain range as stated.

spots.title: Set when the flush gets there
spots.history: BTN opens, you call. Flop: check-call 1.8. Turn Q♥: you check, BTN bets 6.5 (⅔ pot).

villain.label: BTN betting top pair or better plus draws

why: You need {required}.
Bottom set is behind made flushes but has {outs} outs to a full house and is ahead of everything else: {equity}.
With that much equity, raising for value (and to charge one-card flush draws) is strongest; calling is fine; folding is far too tight.
assumptions: Villain range as stated.

spots.title: BB defense with K9o vs a button open
spots.history: BTN opens to 2.5bb, SB folds.

villain.label: BTN 6-max opening range

why: K9o is inside the big blind's defending range (K5o+).
You only need {required} raw equity — you already have 1bb in the pot — and K9o has {equity} vs the button's range.
The source doesn't split calls and 3-bets: calling or 3-betting are both acceptable; folding is too tight.
assumptions: Poker Skill BB-vs-BTN defend chart, 6-max, 100bb.

spots.title: AJo on the button vs a cutoff open
spots.history: CO opens to 2.5bb, folded to you on the button.

villain.label: CO 6-max opening range

why: In the source chart AJo is a call (AQo, AJo, KQo, KJo, QJo flat) rather than a 3-bet.
You have position for the whole hand; AJo is too strong to fold vs a cutoff range ({equity} raw equity) but often dominated by the hands that call a 3-bet.
Price: {required} raw equity needed.
assumptions: Poker Skill BTN-vs-CO chart (simplified, one action per hand).
